lessons.title: What is Linux, really?
lessons.body:
Linux is not a full operating system by itself - it is the KERNEL, the core program that talks to your hardware.

Think of a car: the kernel is the engine. You never drive an engine alone - you need seats, wheels, a steering wheel. A Linux distribution (distro) like Ubuntu or Fedora bundles the kernel with tools and apps so you can actually use it.

When people say 'I use Linux', they mean they use a distro built on the Linux kernel.

lessons.title: A 5-minute history
lessons.body:
1969: Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie build Unix at Bell Labs. It is powerful but expensive and closed.

1983: Richard Stallman starts the GNU project - free Unix-like tools for everyone.

1991: Linus Torvalds, a Finnish student, writes a free kernel 'just for fun' and posts it online. GNU tools + his kernel = what we call Linux today.

Now: every top-500 supercomputer, most web servers, every Android phone and most cloud machines run Linux.

lessons.title: Distros: one kernel, many flavors
lessons.body:
A distribution = Linux kernel + package manager + default apps + a philosophy.

Debian family (Ubuntu, Mint): apt, .deb packages, beginner friendly.
Red Hat family (RHEL, Fedora, AlmaLinux): dnf/yum, .rpm packages, common in companies.
Arch: rolling release, always newest, for enthusiasts.

Interview tip: companies run servers on RHEL-like or Ubuntu LTS systems, so learn apt AND dnf basics.
lessons.diagram:
Linux kernel
                  |
   +----------+---+---------+
   |          |           |
 Debian     Red Hat      Arch
   |          |           |
 Ubuntu    Fedora      Manjaro
 Mint      AlmaLinux

lessons.title: Why companies love Linux
lessons.body:
Free and open source: no license fees, and anyone can read the code - so bugs and security holes get fixed fast.

Stable: servers run for years without rebooting.

Secure by design: users, permissions and a huge reviewing community.

Scriptable: everything can be automated from the command line - which is exactly why system admins and DevOps engineers are hired.
lessons.example:
$ uname -r
5.15.0-91-generic        <- your kernel version

$ cat /etc/os-release
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION="22.04 LTS"    <- your distro

lessons.title: One tree, one root
lessons.body:
Windows has many drives (C:, D:). Linux has ONE tree starting at / (called 'root').

Every file, folder, disk, USB stick and even hardware device hangs somewhere on this single tree. Other disks are 'mounted' (attached) into folders of the tree instead of getting letters.

Once this clicks, everything else in Linux gets easier.
lessons.diagram:
/  <- root, the top of everything
|-- home/     <- users live here (/home/akash)
|-- etc/      <- configuration files
|-- var/      <- logs and changing data
|-- usr/      <- installed programs
|-- tmp/      <- temporary files (wiped on reboot)
|-- dev/      <- hardware as files (/dev/sda = disk)
|-- proc/     <- live kernel info (virtual)
|-- root/     <- home of the admin user

lessons.title: pwd, cd, ls - your three best friends
lessons.body:
pwd = 'where am I?' (print working directory).

cd = 'go somewhere' (change directory). cd /etc goes to /etc, cd .. goes UP one level, cd ~ (or just cd) goes home, cd - goes BACK to where you were.

ls = 'show me what is here'. ls -l shows details, ls -a shows hidden dotfiles, ls -lh shows sizes in K/M/G.
lessons.example:
$ pwd
/home/akash

$ cd /etc/nginx
$ pwd
/etc/nginx

$ cd ..          <- up one level
$ cd ~           <- back home

$ ls -lh
-rw-r--r-- 1 akash akash 4.0K notes.txt

lessons.title: Absolute vs relative paths
lessons.body:
An ABSOLUTE path starts from root: /home/akash/docs/report.txt. It works from anywhere.

A RELATIVE path starts from where you stand: if you are in /home/akash, then docs/report.txt means /home/akash/docs/report.txt.

Special shortcuts: . = this directory, .. = parent directory, ~ = my home.

Rule of thumb: in scripts use absolute paths (scripts can run from anywhere).
lessons.diagram:
you are here: /home/akash

absolute:  /var/log/syslog   (full address)
relative:  ../../var/log/syslog (directions
           from where you stand)

.  = /home/akash   (here)
.. = /home         (one up)

lessons.title: Hidden files and finding things
lessons.body:
Files starting with a dot are hidden: .bashrc, .ssh/. They are normal files - ls just hides them by default. Config for your user usually lives in dotfiles at home.

find = slow but precise search of real files right now.
locate = instant search from a database (updatedb refreshes it).
lessons.example:
$ ls -a ~
.bashrc  .profile  .ssh  notes.txt

$ find /etc -name '*.conf'
/etc/resolv.conf
/etc/sysctl.conf

$ locate nginx.conf
/etc/nginx/nginx.conf

lessons.title: Create, copy, move, delete
lessons.body:
mkdir makes directories (mkdir -p a/b/c makes the whole chain).

touch makes an empty file (or refreshes its timestamp).

cp copies: cp file backup.txt, cp -r dir1 dir2 for folders.

mv moves AND renames - same command, two jobs.

rm deletes FOREVER. There is no recycle bin. Always read the command twice before pressing Enter, especially with rm -r or rm -rf.
lessons.example:
$ mkdir -p projects/demo
$ touch projects/demo/readme.txt
$ cp projects/demo/readme.txt backup.txt
$ mv backup.txt projects/
$ rm -r projects/demo   <- gone, no undo!

lessons.title: Links: shortcuts, Linux style
lessons.body:
A SOFT link (symlink) is like a Windows shortcut - a signpost to another path. Delete the original and the signpost points nowhere (broken link).

A HARD link is a second NAME for the exact same data (same inode). Delete the original name and the data still lives under the other name.

ln -s target linkname makes a symlink; ln target linkname makes a hard link.
lessons.diagram:
symlink:   link.s --> /real/file.txt --> DATA
           (delete file.txt: link.s breaks)

hard link: name1 --+
                   +--> inode 4392 --> DATA
           name2 --+
           (delete name1: data survives)

lessons.title: Find anything: find and du
lessons.body:
find walks the real directory tree: find / -name 'error.log' searches by name, find /home -size +100M hunts big files.

du -sh folder tells you how much space a folder eats - the first command to run when a disk fills up.

file tells you what a file REALLY is, ignoring its extension.
lessons.example:
$ find /var/log -name '*.log' -size +50M
/var/log/bigapp/debug.log

$ du -sh /var/log/*
4.0K   /var/log/apt
812M   /var/log/bigapp

$ file mystery
mystery: PDF document, version 1.4

lessons.title: rm -rf: the command to respect
lessons.body:
rm -rf means: delete EVERYTHING here, recursively, never ask.

The classic disaster is a space in the wrong place: rm -rf / tmp/old (note the space after /) deletes the whole system, not /tmp/old.

Safety habits: use Tab-completion, run ls on the path first, and never run rm -rf as root unless you are 100% sure. In scripts, quote variables: rm -rf "$DIR/"* - an empty unquoted $DIR becomes rm -rf /* .
lessons.diagram:
rm -rf /tmp/old     <- OK: deletes /tmp/old
rm -rf / tmp/old    <- DISASTER: deletes / (everything)
          ^
          one space = your whole server

lessons.title: Reading files: cat, less, head, tail
lessons.body:
cat dumps the whole file - fine for short files.

less opens a pager: scroll with arrows, search with /word, quit with q. This is how pros read logs.

head shows the first lines, tail the last. tail -f is magic: it FOLLOWS a file and shows new lines live - perfect for watching logs while debugging.
lessons.example:
$ head -n 5 /var/log/syslog
Sep 27 08:01 server sshd[911]: ...

$ tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
192.168.1.5 - - [27/Sep] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200
<- new lines appear here in real time

lessons.title: Pipes and redirection
lessons.body:
Small tools, combined. That is the Unix philosophy.

| (pipe) sends one command's output into the next command's input.

> writes output to a file (overwrites). >> appends. 2> captures errors.

With just these, you can build powerful one-liners from simple tools.
lessons.diagram:
ps aux | grep nginx | awk '{print $2}'

ps aux        ->  all processes
grep nginx    ->  only nginx lines
awk '{print $2}' -> only the PID column

command  > out.txt   (overwrite)
command >> out.txt   (append)
command 2> err.txt   (errors only)

lessons.title: grep: find needles in haystacks
lessons.body:
grep PATTERN FILE prints lines matching the pattern.

Daily flags: -i ignore case, -r search folders recursively, -n show line numbers, -v show NON-matching lines, -c count matches.

90% of log debugging is: tail -f the log, or grep -i 'error' the log.
lessons.example:
$ grep -in 'failed' /var/log/auth.log
812:Sep 27 09:12 sshd: Failed password for root

$ grep -ri 'timeout' /etc/nginx/
/etc/nginx/nginx.conf: keepalive_timeout 65;

lessons.title: cut, sort, uniq, wc: data crunching
lessons.body:
cut extracts columns (cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd lists all usernames).

sort orders lines (sort -n for numbers, sort -h for human sizes).

uniq collapses duplicate lines - always sort first, because uniq only merges ADJACENT duplicates.

wc -l counts lines: 'how many users?' = wc -l /etc/passwd.
lessons.example:
$ cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort | head -3
backup
bin
bash

$ history | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
    120 ls
     80 cd
     61 grep   <- your most used commands

lessons.title: Users and groups in plain words
lessons.body:
Every person (and many services) gets a USER. Users are collected into GROUPS so you can give a whole team access at once.

/etc/passwd = the list of users (name, UID, home, shell).
/etc/shadow = password hashes - root only, so attackers can't steal them.
/etc/group = the list of groups.

root (UID 0) is the superuser: it can do anything - which is why we use sudo instead of living as root.
lessons.example:
$ whoami
akash

$ id
uid=1000(akash) gid=1000(akash) groups=1000(akash),27(sudo)

$ getent passwd akash
akash:x:1000:1000:Akash,,,:/home/akash:/bin/bash

lessons.title: Reading rwx like a book
lessons.body:
Every file has three sets of permissions: OWNER, GROUP, OTHERS. Each set has three letters: r (read), w (write), x (execute/enter).

-rw-r--r-- reads: regular file; owner can read+write; group and others can only read.

drwxr-xr-x reads: directory; owner can do everything; others can enter and look but not change.

On a directory, x means 'may enter' - without it you cannot cd in, even with r.
lessons.diagram:
- rw- r-- r--
|  |   |   |
|  |   |   +-- others: read only
|  |   +------ group:  read only
|  +---------- owner:  read + write
+------------- regular file (d=dir, l=link)

r=4  w=2  x=1  ->  7=rwx  6=rw-  5=r-x  4=r--

lessons.title: chmod and chown
lessons.body:
chmod changes PERMISSIONS: chmod 755 script.sh (owner rwx, others rx) or chmod +x script.sh (just add execute).

chown changes OWNERSHIP: chown akash:developers file.txt.

Numbers are just sums: r=4, w=2, x=1. 6 = 4+2 = rw. 5 = 4+1 = r-x.

Classic setups: 644 for normal files, 755 for scripts and directories, 600 for private keys.
lessons.example:
$ chmod +x deploy.sh
$ chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   <- ssh refuses loose keys
$ sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/www/html/index.html

lessons.title: sudo: borrowed superpowers
lessons.body:
sudo runs ONE command as root: sudo apt update. Every use is logged - companies love that.

Who may sudo is decided in /etc/sudoers, edited ONLY with visudo (it syntax-checks before saving; a typo in sudoers can lock everyone out).

On Ubuntu, members of the 'sudo' group may sudo: usermod -aG sudo akash adds him (the -a matters: without it you REPLACE his groups).
lessons.diagram:
normal user --- sudo command ---> runs as root
                    |
              logged in /var/log/auth.log

/etc/sudoers:  akash  ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
               ^user  ^can run anything

lessons.title: What is a process?
lessons.body:
A process is a running program. Open Firefox twice = two processes from one program.

Each process has a PID (process ID) and a parent (PPID). PID 1 - systemd - is the ancestor of everything.

See them: ps aux for a snapshot, top (or htop) for a live view. q quits top.
lessons.diagram:
systemd (PID 1)
  |-- sshd (PID 800)
  |     |-- bash (PID 901)   <- your shell
  |           |-- top (PID 950)
  |-- nginx (PID 820)
  |-- cron (PID 700)

lessons.title: Signals: talking to processes
lessons.body:
A signal is a short message to a process.

SIGTERM (15) = 'please shut down cleanly' - what plain kill sends.
SIGKILL (9) = 'die NOW' - cannot be ignored, unsaved work is lost. Last resort.
SIGINT (2) = Ctrl+C.
SIGTSTP = Ctrl+Z (pause).

kill PID sends TERM; kill -9 PID forces. pkill nginx kills by name.
lessons.example:
$ ps aux | grep python
akash  4242  3.0  ... python app.py

$ kill 4242        <- polite stop
$ kill -9 4242     <- force, only if stuck
$ kill -l | head   <- list all signals

lessons.title: Background jobs: &, jobs, fg, bg
lessons.body:
Append & to start something in the background: ./backup.sh & - your prompt stays free.

jobs lists this shell's background work ([1] Running ...).

fg %1 pulls job 1 back to the foreground. bg %1 resumes a paused job in the background.

Ctrl+Z pauses the foreground program - handy when you started something big and forgot &.

Logging out kills your jobs unless you used nohup or tmux/screen.
lessons.example:
$ ./long-scan.sh &
[1] 5001
$ jobs
[1]+  Running  ./long-scan.sh &
$ fg %1     <- bring it back

lessons.title: Priorities and system health
lessons.body:
nice sets how polite a process is about CPU: -20 (greedy, root only) to 19 (very polite). Start nice: nice -n 10 ./heavy.sh. Change later: renice 5 -p 4242.

Health check trio:
uptime - load average for 1/5/15 minutes (compare with CPU count).
free -h - memory and swap.
df -h - disk space.

These three commands answer 'is the server OK?' in 10 seconds.
lessons.example:
$ uptime
 09:30:01 up 12 days, load average: 0.42, 0.35, 0.30

$ free -h
Mem:   total 7.7Gi   used 3.1Gi   available 4.2Gi
Swap:  total 2.0Gi   used  12Mi

lessons.title: Why package managers are magic
lessons.body:
Installing software by hand means: download, unpack, resolve its dependencies (other packages it needs), copy files, update, remove cleanly... painful.

A package manager does ALL of that in one command, from trusted repositories (repos) - servers full of tested packages.

Debian/Ubuntu: apt with .deb files. RHEL/Fedora: dnf (old name yum) with .rpm files. Arch: pacman.
lessons.diagram:
you:  sudo apt install nginx
                    |
                    v
   repo server (packages + metadata)
                    |
      downloads nginx + its dependencies
                    |
        installs files in the right places
                    |
         tracks everything for clean removal

lessons.title: apt: your daily four
lessons.body:
sudo apt update - refresh the catalog (what versions exist). No software changes yet.

sudo apt upgrade - install the newer versions. update first, upgrade second, always.

sudo apt install nginx - install something new, dependencies included.

sudo apt remove nginx - uninstall (configs stay). apt purge also deletes configs. apt autoremove cleans orphaned dependencies.
lessons.example:
$ sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
...
$ apt show nginx | head -4
Package: nginx
Version: 1.18.0-0ubuntu1
$ dpkg -l | grep nginx   <- is it installed?

lessons.title: dnf / rpm on the Red Hat side
lessons.body:
Interviews love asking both families - here is the mirror:

apt install  ->  dnf install
apt remove   ->  dnf remove
apt update   ->  dnf check-update
dpkg -l      ->  rpm -qa (query all)
dpkg -i x.deb ->  rpm -ivh x.rpm

Which package owns /usr/bin/curl? dpkg -S (Debian) or rpm -qf (Red Hat).
lessons.example:
$ sudo dnf install httpd -y
$ rpm -qa | grep httpd
httpd-2.4.57-1.el9.x86_64
$ rpm -qf /usr/sbin/httpd
httpd-2.4.57-1.el9.x86_64

lessons.title: When packages fight: fixing breakage
lessons.body:
Half-finished installs leave 'broken dependencies'. The fix is almost always: sudo apt --fix-broken install (apt -f install) - apt computes what to add or remove to heal the system.

Extra repos live in /etc/apt/sources.list and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ - check there when a package is 'not found'.

Snaps and Flatpaks are sandboxed, distro-independent packages - useful for desktop apps, less so for servers.
lessons.example:
$ sudo apt --fix-broken install
Reading package lists... Done
The following packages will be REMOVED: ...
$ cat /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list

lessons.title: ip: your network x-ray
lessons.body:
ip addr (short: ip a) shows your interfaces and their IP addresses.

ip route shows where traffic goes - the 'default via ...' line is your gateway (the router).

The old command was ifconfig - know it, but use ip.

Quick check when the network 'is down': ip a (do I have an IP?) -> ip route (do I have a gateway?) -> ping the gateway -> ping 8.8.8.8 -> ping google.com.
lessons.example:
$ ip a
2: eth0: inet 192.168.1.50/24 ...

$ ip route
default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0

lessons.title: ping, DNS and the /etc/hosts trick
lessons.body:
ping 8.8.8.8 tests raw connectivity (numbers). ping google.com ALSO tests DNS (names). If numbers work but names fail - DNS is broken: look at /etc/resolv.conf.

DNS = the internet's phone book: name -> IP, on port 53. dig google.com shows the full answer.

/etc/hosts is your private mini-DNS, checked first. Admins add test entries there; malware also abuses it.
lessons.diagram:
browser:  google.com ?
             |
   /etc/hosts? --yes--> use that IP
      | no
   DNS server (53) --> 142.250.x.x
             |
        connection!

lessons.title: Ports and services: who is listening?
lessons.body:
A port is a numbered door on an IP address. IP = building, port = apartment.

Famous doors: 22 SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 53 DNS, 3306 MySQL.

ss -tuln lists every open door on your server (t=tcp, u=udp, l=listening, n=numeric). If the web site is down but nginx runs, ss tells you whether anything listens on 80 at all.

A firewall (ufw, firewalld) decides which doors are open to the world.
lessons.example:
$ ss -tuln
State  Local Address:Port
LISTEN 0.0.0.0:22
LISTEN 0.0.0.0:80

$ sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
$ sudo ufw enable

lessons.title: ssh: your remote hands
lessons.body:
ssh user@server logs you into a remote machine, encrypted. This is THE daily tool of every admin.

scp file user@server:/path copies files over the same encrypted channel.

Port changed? ssh -p 2222 user@server (lowercase p for ssh, CAPITAL P for scp - classic interview trap).
lessons.example:
$ ssh akash@192.168.1.10
akash@server:~$ hostname
server

$ scp report.pdf akash@192.168.1.10:/tmp/
report.pdf   100%  220KB

lessons.title: df and du: the space detectives
lessons.body:
'Disk full' is the most common server emergency ever. Two commands solve it:

df -h shows each FILESYSTEM's total/used/free - tells you WHICH disk is full.

du -sh /some/dir shows one folder's size - tells you WHAT ate it. Combine with sort to find the biggest folders.

Also watch inodes (df -i): millions of tiny files can fill a disk's file-index while space remains.
lessons.example:
$ df -h
/dev/sda1  50G  49G  0G  100% /

$ du -h --max-depth=1 /var | sort -h | tail -3
1.2G  /var/lib
6.8G  /var/log   <- found the eater

lessons.title: mount: attaching disks to the tree
lessons.body:
A new disk is invisible until you: partition it (fdisk/parted), format it (mkfs.ext4), and MOUNT it (attach it to a folder): mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data.

umount detaches (yes, one 'n'). It refuses while files are open - find the holders with lsof or fuser.

/etc/fstab lists mounts to apply at boot. Use UUIDs there (from blkid) because /dev/sdb can become /dev/sdc after a reboot.
lessons.example:
$ lsblk
sdb    8:16  0  100G  0 disk
+-sdb1 8:17  0 100G  0 part

$ sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
$ sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/data
$ blkid /dev/sdb1
/dev/sdb1: UUID="9f3a-..."  <- put this in fstab

lessons.title: LVM: flexible storage
lessons.body:
Plain partitions are rigid: want it bigger later? Painful.

LVM adds a flexible layer: Physical Volumes (disks) pool into a Volume Group, and you carve Logical Volumes from the pool - resize them live while the server runs.

Grow in two steps: lvextend -L +10G /dev/data/web (bigger LV), then resize2fs /dev/data/web (grow the ext4 inside).
lessons.diagram:
/dev/sdb  /dev/sdc
   |          |
 pvcreate   pvcreate
   +----+----+
        v
   VG 'data'  (vgcreate)
        |
  +-----+------+
  |            |
 LV 'web'    LV 'db'   (lvcreate)
  |            |
 mkfs.ext4  mkfs.ext4

lessons.title: RAID and inodes
lessons.body:
RAID 1 = mirroring: two disks hold identical data, one can die with zero loss. RAID 0 = striping: speed, but one disk dying kills everything. RAID is NOT backup - rm deletes from both disks instantly!

An inode is a file's ID card: permissions, owner, timestamps, where the data blocks are. The NAME is stored separately in the directory, pointing at the inode - that is why hard links (two names, one inode) work.
lessons.diagram:
RAID 1 (mirror):        RAID 0 (stripe):
disk1 == disk2          disk1 + disk2 = fast
one dies, you survive   one dies, all lost

inode 4392: { perms, owner, size, blocks }
  ^        ^
  |        |
name1    name2   (hard links)

lessons.title: Your first script in 2 minutes
lessons.body:
A script is commands in a file, run top to bottom.

1. First line: #!/bin/bash (the shebang - which interpreter to use).
2. Make it runnable: chmod +x myscript.sh.
3. Run it: ./myscript.sh.

Comments start with #. Write them - future-you says thanks.
lessons.example:
#!/bin/bash
# Say hello and show the date

echo "Hello, Akash!"
date

$ chmod +x hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh
Hello, Akash!
Sat Sep 27 13:50 IST 2026

lessons.title: Variables and arguments
lessons.body:
Variables: NAME=value (NO spaces around =), read with $NAME. Quote on use: "$NAME" keeps spaces safe.

Command substitution: TODAY=$(date +%F) captures a command's output.

Arguments: $1, $2 are what you pass after the script name; $# is how many; $@ is all of them; $0 is the script's own name.

$? holds the last command's exit code: 0 = success, anything else = failure.
lessons.example:
#!/bin/bash
NAME=$1
echo "Backup for $NAME"
mkdir -p "backups/$NAME"
echo "args: $# | last exit code: $?"

$ ./backup.sh website
Backup for website
args: 1 | last exit code: 0

lessons.title: Decisions: if, test, case
lessons.body:
if [ condition ]; then ... fi makes choices.

String test: [ "$a" = "yes" ]. Number tests: -eq -ne -lt -gt. File tests: -f (file exists), -d (directory), -x (executable). Mind the spaces inside [ ] - they are required.

For menus (start|stop|restart) case is cleaner than many ifs.

lessons.title: Loops and real-world script hygiene
lessons.body:
for name in list; do ...; done repeats per item. while condition; do ...; done repeats while true - while read -r line is THE way to process a file line by line.

Pro habits:
set -e at the top: stop on first error instead of plowing through a broken run.
bash -x script.sh: trace mode - prints every command as it runs; your best debugging friend.
Quote every variable: "$file" not $file - spaces in names break unquoted scripts.
lessons.example:
while read -r user; do
  echo "Checking $user"
done < users.txt

for srv in web1 web2 db1; do
  ping -c1 $srv > /dev/null && echo "$srv OK"
done

lessons.title: How a Linux machine boots
lessons.body:
Power on -> firmware (BIOS/UEFI) checks hardware and finds a bootable disk -> the bootloader (GRUB) loads the kernel into memory -> the kernel starts PID 1: systemd -> systemd starts all services in parallel (network, ssh, nginx...) -> login prompt.

Knowing this chain tells you WHERE to debug: no GRUB = disk/bootloader issue; GRUB but no login = service issue.
lessons.diagram:
POWER
  |
  v
BIOS/UEFI (firmware)
  |
  v
GRUB (bootloader)
  |
  v
Linux kernel
  |
  v
systemd (PID 1) ----> sshd, nginx, cron...
  |
  v
login prompt

lessons.title: systemctl: the remote control
lessons.body:
start / stop / restart act NOW: sudo systemctl restart nginx.

enable / disable control BOOT behavior: enable adds nginx to startup.

enable --now does both at once - the common answer to 'make it run and survive reboot'.

status shows running state + recent logs: systemctl status nginx. is-active and is-enabled answer yes/no questions for scripts.
lessons.example:
$ sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/nginx.service

$ systemctl is-active nginx
active
$ systemctl status nginx | head -3
* nginx.service - A high performance web server
   Active: active (running)

lessons.title: Unit files: services as text
lessons.body:
A service is just a text file (a 'unit'). Package defaults live in /usr/lib/systemd/system/, your overrides belong in /etc/systemd/system/.

Three sections: [Unit] describes and orders (After=network.target), [Service] says how to run (ExecStart=, Restart=), [Install] wires it to boot (WantedBy=multi-user.target).

After ANY edit: sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then restart the service.

mask (vs disable) forbids starting entirely - even manually - until unmask.
lessons.example:
[Unit]
Description=My backup service
After=network.target

[Service]
ExecStart=/opt/backup/run.sh
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

lessons.title: journalctl: every log in one place
lessons.body:
systemd collects service logs into the journal. journalctl reads it.

The daily trio:
journalctl -u nginx - logs of ONE service.
journalctl -f - follow live, like tail -f.
journalctl -b - only since this boot; -b -1 shows the PREVIOUS boot (gold after a crash/reboot).

Add -p err to see only errors, --since '1 hour ago' for a time window.
lessons.example:
$ journalctl -u nginx -n 5 --no-pager
Sep 27 13:10 server nginx[820]: started
...
$ journalctl -p err -b
<- errors of this boot only

lessons.title: SSH keys: passwords done right
lessons.body:
Passwords can be guessed; keys practically cannot.

ssh-keygen creates a PAIR on your machine: a private key (never leaves your laptop, chmod 600) and a public key (safe to share).

ssh-copy-id user@server installs your public key into the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. From then on, login needs no password.

Server hardening classic: PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config - then reload sshd. Test in a SECOND session before closing your first!
lessons.example:
$ ssh-keygen -t ed25519
$ ssh-copy-id akash@server
$ ssh akash@server   <- no password!

$ sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitRootLogin no
$ sudo systemctl reload ssh

lessons.title: cron: the robot alarm clock
lessons.body:
cron runs commands on a schedule. crontab -e edits YOUR schedule; five time fields decide when: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

0 2 * * * = 2 AM daily (backup o'clock). */5 * * * * = every 5 minutes. @daily, @weekly, @reboot are shortcuts.

System jobs live in /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.daily and friends. Scripts should use absolute paths - cron's environment is minimal.

lessons.title: tar, gzip, rsync: pack and move
lessons.body:
tar packs many files into one archive: -czf creates gzipped, -xzf extracts, -tzf lists without extracting. Remember: Create, eXtract, lisT.

rsync is the smart copier: rsync -av /data/ server:/backup/ copies only what CHANGED and preserves permissions. It is the backbone of real backup scripts. The trailing slash matters: /data/ copies the CONTENTS, /data copies the FOLDER itself.
lessons.example:
$ tar -czf etc-backup.tar.gz /etc
$ tar -tzf etc-backup.tar.gz | head -3
etc/
etc/hostname

$ rsync -av /var/www/ backup:/srv/www/
sending incremental file list
index.html

lessons.title: Logs, logins and least privilege
lessons.body:
/var/log is the diary of the system: auth.log (Debian) or secure (RHEL) records logins - check it after 'something feels off'. last shows login history; who shows who is on RIGHT now.

Golden rule: least privilege - every user and service gets ONLY the access it needs. Web servers run as www-data, not root; humans use sudo, not root shells.

And the habit that beats all tools: apply security updates regularly. Most real-world hacks exploit old, already-fixed bugs.
lessons.example:
$ last | head -3
akash  pts/0  192.168.1.5  Sat Sep 27 13:00 still logged in

$ grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log | wc -l
412   <- someone is knocking; consider fail2ban
